title: Computable Parameterized Bisection Definitions
content: Three computable definitions encode the oracle-parameterized bisection algorithm. paramBisectStep takes a pair (left, right) and a Bool choice c: if c=true it takes the right half [mid, right]; if c=false it takes the left half [left, mid]. paramBisect iterates this n times using an oracle sequence choices : ℕ → Bool. paramBisectMid extracts the midpoint. Crucially, all three are regular def (not noncomputable) — the oracle supplies branch decisions instead of computing 'if f(mid) ≤ 0'.
mathContext:
$\text{paramBisect}(\text{choices}, 0, p) = p$
$\text{paramBisect}(\text{choices}, n+1, p) = \text{paramBisectStep}(\text{paramBisect}(\text{choices}, n, p),\, \text{choices}(n))$

title: Width Formula: (b-a)/2^n — No Classical Logic
content: paramBisect_width proves that after n bisection steps with any choice sequence, the interval width equals exactly (b-a)/2^n. The proof uses induction: the base case is immediate; the inductive step rewrites via paramBisectStep_width (which holds by cases on Bool) and then uses ring. No Classical.em or Classical.choice appears — Bool case analysis is fully computable.

title: SignConsistent Oracle and Sign Invariant
content: SignConsistent f choices p n asserts that the oracle choices correctly records f's sign at each midpoint: choices(k) = true iff f(mid_k) ≤ 0. This is a HYPOTHESIS about the oracle — it is never proved constructively (decidability of real comparisons is not available in general). Given SignConsistent, paramBisect_sign proves the sign invariant: f(left_n) ≤ 0 ≤ f(right_n) holds for all n. The proof is by induction, case-splitting on the Bool choice and using the consistency hypothesis directly — no classical reasoning required.

title: Width Converges to Zero
content: paramBisect_width_tendsto_zero proves that the interval widths tend to 0 as n → ∞ for any choice sequence. The proof rewrites width as (b-a)·(1/2)^n pointwise (avoiding a simp loop between div/inv), then applies tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one since |1/2| < 1. This step requires no classical axioms beyond those implicit in ℝ's topology.

title: Endpoint Convergence — Classical Boundary
content: paramBisect_endpoints_converge proves that the left and right endpoints converge to a common limit. This is where Classical.choice enters: Mathlib's tendsto_atTop_ciSup and tendsto_atTop_ciInf use completeness of ℝ (the supremum/infimum of a bounded monotone/antitone sequence). The proof constructs xl = ⊔ left_n and xr = ⊓ right_n, proves they tend to their respective limits, then shows xl = xr using the width-to-zero fact. This is the first classically non-constructive step.
mathContext: $x_L = \sup_n l_n,\ x_R = \inf_n r_n,\ \text{and } x_R - x_L = \lim_{n}(r_n - l_n) = 0 \Rightarrow x_L = x_R$

title: Root Theorem: Limit is a Root
content: bisection_limit_is_root proves that if f is continuous, the choices are sign-consistent, and x is the left-endpoint limit, then f(x) = 0. The proof uses le_of_tendsto and ge_of_tendsto: since f(left_n) ≤ 0 for all n and left_n → x continuously, we get f(x) ≤ 0; similarly f(x) ≥ 0 from the right endpoints. Hence f(x) = 0.
mathContext: $f(l_n) \leq 0 \leq f(r_n) \text{ and } l_n, r_n \to x \Rightarrow f(x) \leq 0 \text{ and } f(x) \geq 0 \Rightarrow f(x) = 0$

title: Main Theorem: Constructive vs Classical Boundary
content: constructive_vs_classical_ivt assembles all results into a single conjunction that precisely characterizes where classical logic enters bisection-based IVT proofs. Three parts are constructive (no Classical.em or Classical.choice): the exact width formula, sign invariant preservation under an oracle, and width-to-zero. One part is classical: endpoint convergence (requires Classical.choice via completeness). The proof term is a direct application of the component theorems.
mathContext: Parts (1)–(3): provable in Bishop-style constructive mathematics. Part (4): requires the law of excluded middle for real comparisons (or Classical.choice via completeness).
prerequisites: all prior theorems in this file
